plain_english: When you know your place in life, you don't chase things that are beyond you. So what do you actually want to happen to you? I'm content if I want and avoid things naturally. I'm content if I move toward and away from things as nature designed me to do. I'm content with my choices and decisions and judgments. So why do you strut around like you've got a stick up your back? My wish has always been for people to meet me and admire me. I want followers to shout, "What a great philosopher!" But who are these people you want to admire you? Aren't they the same people you usually call crazy? So you want crazy people to admire you?
original_excerpt: When a man holds his proper station in life, he does not gape after things beyond it. Man, what do you wish to happen to you? I am satisfied if I desire and avoid conformably to nature, if I employ movements towards and from an object as I am by nature formed to do, and purpose and design and assent. Why then do you strut before us as if you had swallowed a spit? My wish has always been that those who meet me should admire me, and those who follow me should exclaim, O the great philosopher! Who are they by whom you wish to be admired? Are they not those of whom you are used to say that they are mad? Well, then, do you wish to be admired by madmen?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1

plain_english: Everyone shares the same basic ideas about what's good and right. These basic ideas don't contradict each other. Who among us doesn't believe that Good is useful and worth choosing? Who doesn't believe we should always follow and pursue it? Who doesn't assume that Justice is beautiful and proper? So where do disagreements come from? They come when we try to apply these basic ideas to specific situations. One person says, "He did well — he's brave." Another says, "No, he acted foolishly." That's when disputes start. This is what Jews, Syrians, Egyptians, and Romans argue about. They don't disagree that holiness should come first in all cases. They disagree about whether eating pork is holy or unholy.
original_excerpt: ON PRÆCOGNITIONS.—Præcognitions are common to all men, and præcognition is not contradictory to præcognition. For who of us does not assume that Good is useful and eligible, and in all circumstances that we ought to follow and pursue it? And who of us does not assume that Justice is beautiful and becoming? When then does the contradiction arise? It arises in the adaptation of the præcognitions to the particular cases. When one man says, "He has done well; he is a brave man," and another says, "Not so; but he has acted foolishly," then the disputes arise among men. This is the dispute among the Jews and the Syrians and the Egyptians and the Romans; not whether holiness should be preferred to all things and in all cases should be pursued, but whether it is holy to eat pig's flesh or not holy.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1

plain_english: You'll see this same argument between Agamemnon and Achilles. Let's bring them forward. What do you say, Agamemnon? Should we do what's proper and right? "Absolutely." And what about you, Achilles? Don't you agree that we should do what's good? "I absolutely do." Then apply your basic beliefs to this specific situation. Here's where the fight starts. Agamemnon says, "I shouldn't have to give Chryseis back to her father." Achilles says, "Yes, you should." One of them is clearly misapplying their basic understanding of what "should" or "duty" means. Then Agamemnon says, "Well, if I have to give back Chryseis, then it's only fair that I take someone else's prize from one of you." Achilles replies, "So you'd take the woman I love?" "Yes, the one you love." "So I'm the only one who gets nothing? I'm the only one who loses his prize?" That's how the argument starts.
original_excerpt: You will find this dispute also between Agamemnon and Achilles; for call them forth. What do you say, Agamemnon? ought not that to be done which is proper and right? "Certainly." Well, what do you say, Achilles? do you not admit that what is good ought to be done? "I do most certainly." Adapt your præcognitions then to the present matter. Here the dispute begins. Agamemnon says, "I ought not to give up Chryseis to her father." Achilles says, "You ought." It is certain that one of the two makes a wrong adaptation of the præcognition of "ought" or "duty." Further, Agamemnon says, "Then if I ought to restore Chryseis, it is fit that I take his prize from some of you." Achilles replies, "Would you then take her whom I love?" "Yes, her whom you love." "Must I then be the only man who goes without a prize? and must I be the only man who has no prize?" Thus the dispute begins.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1

plain_english: So what is education? Education is learning how to use your natural instincts about right and wrong on specific situations in the right way. Then you learn to tell the difference between what's up to you and what isn't. What's up to you: your choices and everything that comes from your choices. What's not up to you: your body, body parts, possessions, parents, siblings, children, country, and basically everyone you deal with. So where should we put what's truly good? What should we base it on? The things that are up to us? But wait — isn't health good? Aren't strong limbs good? Isn't life good? Aren't children and parents and country good? Who's going to listen to you if you say they're not?
original_excerpt: What then is education? Education is the learning how to adapt the natural præcognitions to the particular things conformably to nature; and then to distinguish that of things some are in our power, but others are not. In our power are will and all acts which depend on the will; things not in our power are the body, the parts of the body, possessions, parents, brothers, children, country, and, generally, all with whom we live in society. In what then should we place the good? To what kind of things ([Greek: ousia]) shall we adapt it? To the things which are in our power? Is not health then a good thing, and soundness of limb, and life, and are not children and parents and country? Who will tolerate you if you deny this?
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1

plain_english: Let's apply this idea of "good" to material things and see what happens. If someone suffers loss and doesn't get the good things they want, can they be happy? No way. Can they behave properly toward other people? No. Here's why: I'm naturally wired to look out for myself. If owning land is good for me, then it's also good for me to steal it from my neighbor. If having clothes is good for me, then it's also good for me to steal them from the bathhouse. This is how wars start. This is where civil unrest comes from. Tyrannies. Conspiracies. And how could I still do my duty to Zeus? If I'm suffering and unlucky, he's not taking care of me. What good is he to me if he can't help? What good is he if he lets me stay in this miserable condition? Now I start to hate him. So why do we build temples? Why put up statues of Zeus — or even of evil spirits like Fever? How can Zeus be our Savior, the rain-bringer, the fruit-giver? The truth is, if we say that Good is found in these external things, all of this mess follows.
original_excerpt: Let us then transfer the notion of good to these things. Is it possible, then, when a man sustains damage and does not obtain good things, that he can be happy? It is not possible. And can he maintain towards society a proper behavior? He can not. For I am naturally formed to look after my own interest. If it is my interest to have an estate in land, it is my interest also to take it from my neighbor. If it is my interest to have a garment, it is my interest also to steal it from the bath. This is the origin of wars, civil commotions, tyrannies, conspiracies. And how shall I be still able to maintain my duty towards Zeus? For if I sustain damage and am unlucky, he takes no care of me. And what is he to me if he cannot help me? And further, what is he to me if he allows me to be in the condition in which I am? I now begin to hate him. Why then do we build temples, why setup statues to Zeus, as well as to evil demons, such as to Fever; and how is Zeus the Saviour, and how the giver of rain, and the giver of fruits? And in truth if we place the nature of Good in any such things, all this follows.
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1

plain_english: So what should we do? This is what a real philosopher struggles with. Right now I don't know what's good or bad. Am I crazy? Yes. But suppose I say that good things are found only in what we can control. Everyone will laugh at me. Some old rich guy with gold rings will shake his head and say: "Listen, kid. It's fine to study philosophy, but you need some common sense too. What you're doing is ridiculous. You learn logic from philosophers, but you don't know how to live as well as they do." Man, why are you blaming me if I actually know something? What should I say to this fool? If I stay quiet, he'll explode. I have to say this: "Forgive me, like you'd forgive someone in love. I'm not in control of myself. I'm mad."
original_excerpt: What should we do then? This is the inquiry of the true philosopher who is in labor. Now I do not see what the good is nor the bad. Am I not mad? Yes. But suppose that I place the good somewhere among the things which depend on the will; all will laugh at me. There will come some greyhead wearing many gold rings on his fingers, and he will shake his head and say: "Hear, my child. It is right that you should philosophize; but you ought to have some brains also; all this that you are doing is silly. You learn the syllogism from philosophers; but you know how to act better than philosophers do." Man why then do you blame me, if I know? What shall I say to this slave? If I am silent, he will burst. I must speak in this way: "Excuse me, as you would excuse lovers; I am not my own master; I am mad."
source_reference: Discourses, Against Those Who Wish to Be Admired, Section 1
